content: 1. The correlation between achieving certain antibody titers after vaccination and immunity is well-established at the population level. However, reaching specific antibody thresholds, such as a hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) titer of 32 or 40, does not reliably predict protection against infection at the individual level. 2. Live attenuated influenza vaccines (LAIV) induce lower levels of serum antibodies compared to inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV). However, LAIV is more effective in stimulating cellular immune responses than IIV. 3. The extent of this difference in immune response between LAIV and IIV varies between adults and children. 4. A study involving children aged 6 months to 9 years and adults aged 22 to 49 years demonstrated a significant increase in influenza A-specific interferon-γ-producing CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells in children following LAIV administration, but not after IIV administration. No significant increase in these parameters was observed in adults following either vaccine. 5. Antibodies elicited by vaccination are generally strain-specific, meaning that antibodies against one influenza virus type or subtype provide limited or no protection against other types or subtypes. They also do not protect against antigenic variants of the same virus that arise due to antigenic drift. 6. Cellular immune responses, which may target more conserved viral epitopes, have the potential to provide broader heterosubtypic immunity. 7. Administration of the 2007–2008 seasonal influenza vaccine to adults enhanced T-cell responses to both seasonal and pandemic 2009 (H1N1) hemagglutinin (HA). This effect was significantly greater with LAIV compared to IIV. 8. Among children aged 6 to 35 months, LAIV (but not IIV) induced T-cell responses to highly conserved viral peptides. 9. The composition of influenza vaccines is updated annually, with one or more vaccine strains replaced to protect against viruses anticipated to circulate in the upcoming season. 10. Evidence from clinical trials suggests that protection against antigenically similar viruses to those in the vaccine lasts at least 6–8 months, particularly in non-elderly populations. 11. In some cases, immunity may persist for longer durations if circulating influenza virus strains remain antigenically similar across multiple seasons. For example, three years after vaccination with the A/Hong Kong/68 pandemic vaccine, effectiveness was 67% against influenza caused by the A/Hong Kong/68 virus. 12. Randomized trials among healthy college students showed that IIV provided 92% and 100% efficacy against influenza H3N2 and H1N1 illnesses, respectively, during the first year after vaccination. Without revaccination, there was a 68% reduction in H1N1 illness during the second year when H1N1 was the predominant circulating virus. 13. In a similar study conducted in 1986–1987, IIV reduced influenza A (H1N1) illness by 75% in the first year, reduced H3N2 illness by 45% in the second year, and reduced H1N1 illness by 61% in the third year after vaccination. 14. Serum HAI influenza antibodies and nasal IgA induced by LAIV remain detectable in children for over one year after vaccination. 15. A community-based, nonrandomized open-label trial demonstrated continued protection against medically attended acute respiratory illness (MAARI) during the 2000–2001 influenza season in children who received a single dose of LAIV during the previous 1999–2000 season. 16. A review of four trials (three randomized blinded and one open-label) of LAIV in children aged 6 months to 18 years reported that efficacy against A (H1N1) and A (H3N2) was similar at 9–12 months post-vaccination compared to 1–<5 months post-vaccination. For B strains, efficacy remained comparable at 5–7 months post-vaccination. 17. Two randomized trials and one open-label study reported residual efficacy of LAIV through a second season without revaccination, although at lower levels than observed in the first season. 18. Adults aged ≥65 years typically exhibit diminished immune responses to influenza vaccination compared to healthy younger adults. 19. A review of published literature concluded that there is no clear evidence that vaccine-induced antibody levels decline more rapidly in the elderly. 20. A case-control study conducted in Navarre, Spain, during the 2011–2012 season revealed a decline in vaccine effectiveness from 61% during the first 100 days post-vaccination to 42% for days 110–119, and to -35% thereafter. This decline primarily affected individuals aged ≥65 years. 21. Among persons aged ≥65 years, vaccine effectiveness declined from 85% to 24% to -208% over the same time intervals. However, most viruses isolated from infected vaccinees did not match the vaccine strains. 22. The wide confidence intervals surrounding these estimates indicate the need for larger studies to better characterize potential declines in vaccine effectiveness throughout the season. 23. Limited data suggest that administering additional vaccine doses during the same season does not enhance the antibody response among elderly vaccinees. 24. Inactivated influenza vaccines (IIV), administered via intramuscular or intradermal injection, contain non-replicating virus. Their immunogenicity, efficacy, and effectiveness have been evaluated in children and adults, although fewer randomized studies are available for certain age groups, such as those aged ≥65 years. 25. Children aged ≥6 months typically develop protective antibody levels against specific influenza virus strains after receiving the recommended number of doses of seasonal inactivated influenza vaccine. 26. Immunogenicity studies using the influenza A (H1N1) 2009 monovalent vaccine indicated that 80%–95% of vaccinated children developed protective antibody levels to the 2009 H1N1 influenza virus after two doses. After one dose, the response was 50% for children aged 6–35 months and 75% for those aged 3–9 years. 27. Studies involving seasonal inactivated influenza vaccine in young children have demonstrated that two vaccine doses provide better protection than one dose during the first season a child is vaccinated. 28. In a study of children aged 5–8 years receiving trivalent inactivated vaccine (TIV) for the first time, the proportion of children with protective antibody responses was significantly higher after two doses than after one dose for each antigen. 29. Vaccine effectiveness is lower among children aged <5 years who have never received influenza vaccine previously or who received only one dose in their first year of vaccination compared to children who received two doses in their first year of being vaccinated. 30. Two retrospective studies of children who received only one dose of IIV in their first year of vaccination found no decrease in influenza-like illness (ILI)-related office visits compared to unvaccinated children. 31. 32. These findings support the recommendation that all children aged 6 months through 8 years being vaccinated for the first time should receive two vaccine doses separated by at least four weeks.
